name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q01 - Electron transfer process in the Daniell cell

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates the electrochemical setup of a Daniell cell:

Based on the electrochemical principles shown in the diagram, which statement correctly identifies the nature and polarity of the electrodes and the processes occurring at them?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Conditions and Electrode Arrangement
The diagram depicts a standard Daniell cell comprising a zinc electrode dipping in an aqueous zinc sulfate solution and a copper electrode dipping in an aqueous copper sulfate solution, linked externally by a metallic wire and internally by an agar-agar salt bridge.

Step 2: Identification of Half-Cell Processes
Zinc metal has a higher electron-releasing tendency than copper (\(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -0.76\mathrm{\ V}\) and \(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\mathrm{\ V}\)). Consequently, zinc spontaneously loses electrons to undergo oxidation:
\(\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\).
By definition, the electrode at which oxidation occurs is the anode. In a galvanic cell, electrons accumulate at this electrode, giving the anode a negative electrical polarity.

Step 3: Identification of Cathode Process
The electrons released by zinc travel through the external metallic wire toward the copper electrode. Copper(II) ions in the solution accept these electrons and are reduced to deposit metallic copper:
\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{s})\).
By definition, the electrode at which reduction takes place is the cathode. In a galvanic cell, consumption of electrons makes the cathode the positive pole.

Step 4: Electron Flow versus Conventional Current Flow
Electrons flow spontaneously through the external circuit from the negative zinc anode to the positive copper cathode. By convention, electric current flows in the opposite direction, from the copper cathode to the zinc anode.

Step 5: Final Answer
Zinc acts as the anode with negative polarity where oxidation takes place, whereas copper acts as the cathode with positive polarity where reduction takes place.

answer.text: Zinc acts as the anode with negative polarity where oxidation occurs, while copper acts as the cathode with positive polarity where reduction occurs.
Zinc acts as the cathode with positive polarity where reduction occurs, while copper acts as the anode with negative polarity where oxidation occurs.
Zinc acts as the anode with positive polarity where oxidation occurs, while copper acts as the cathode with negative polarity where reduction occurs.
Both electrodes undergo reduction, with zinc being negatively charged and copper being positively charged.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q02 - Observation and inference in zinc copper displacement

questiontext.text:
The diagram below displays the sequential stages of an experiment in which a metallic zinc strip is immersed in an aqueous solution of copper nitrate:

Which of the following inferences correctly explains the chemical transformation and the test used to confirm the species present in the final colourless solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Visual Description and Experimental Conditions
Initially, the beaker contains an aqueous copper nitrate solution possessing a characteristic blue colour due to hydrated \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions. A clean metallic zinc rod is placed into this solution. As time progresses, the intensity of the blue colour gradually diminishes and a reddish-brown crust accumulates on the zinc rod. In the final stage, the solution becomes completely colourless.

Step 2: Identification of Redox Transformation
Zinc is higher than copper in the activity series, meaning zinc metal has a greater tendency to lose electrons. Zinc undergoes oxidation to enter the aqueous phase as colourless zinc ions:
\(\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\).
Simultaneously, \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions in solution consume the released electrons and undergo reduction to metallic copper:
\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{s})\).
The disappearance of the blue colour marks the near-total reduction of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions, while the reddish coating corresponds to deposited copper metal.

Step 3: Confirmatory Chemical Test for Product Ions
According to the textbook description, when hydrogen sulfide gas (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\)) is passed through the resulting colourless solution made alkaline with ammonia, a characteristic white precipitate of zinc sulfide (\(\mathrm{ZnS}\)) forms:
\(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{S}^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnS}(\mathrm{s})\).
This provides definitive chemical confirmation of the presence of \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions in the colourless solution.

Step 4: Equilibrium State
When copper metal is tested in zinc sulfate solution, no reverse reaction takes place, and no copper ions can be detected even with the highly sensitive sulfide test. This proves that the state of equilibrium for \(\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{s})\) greatly favours the products.

Step 5: Final Answer
Copper(II) ions are reduced to reddish metallic copper while zinc is oxidised to colourless zinc ions, which can be identified by the formation of white zinc sulfide precipitate on passing hydrogen sulfide gas in an alkaline medium.

answer.text: Zinc is reduced to form a reddish coating while copper(II) ions are oxidised to colourless copper(III) ions in solution.

Copper(II) ions are reduced to reddish metallic copper while zinc is oxidised to colourless zinc ions, which form a white precipitate of zinc sulfide upon treatment with hydrogen sulfide in alkaline medium.
The blue colour disappears because copper nitrate decomposes into volatile nitrogen dioxide gas, leaving suspended metallic zinc.
Zinc metal acts as an oxidising agent by accepting two electrons from copper(II) ions to produce black cupric sulfide directly.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q03 - Relative electron releasing tendency of copper and silver

questiontext.text:
The diagram below depicts the progression of an experiment in which a metallic copper strip is dipped into an aqueous silver nitrate solution:

From the observed changes and the reaction occurring in the beaker, what deduction can be drawn regarding the relative electron-releasing tendency of the metals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Visual Progression Analysis
Initially, metallic copper is placed into a clear, colourless solution of silver nitrate (\(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\)). As the reaction proceeds, the solution acquires a distinct blue coloration that intensifies over time, while a glistening layer of metallic silver precipitates on the surface of the copper rod.

Step 2: Governing Chemical Reaction
The net ionic redox equation for the process is:
\(\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{Ag}^+(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})\).
Metallic copper undergoes oxidation by losing two electrons to form hydrated cupric ions (\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\)), which impart the characteristic blue colour to the solution:
\(\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\).
Simultaneously, silver ions in solution accept these electrons and undergo reduction to deposit elemental silver:
\(2\mathrm{Ag}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})\).

Step 3: Comparison of Electron-Releasing Tendencies
Because metallic copper spontaneously donates electrons to silver ions, copper has a stronger tendency to lose electrons (act as a reductant) than silver does. Thus, the electron-releasing tendency follows the order: \(\mathrm{Cu} > \mathrm{Ag}\).

Step 4: Integration with Metal Activity Series
In the earlier displacement experiment, zinc was shown to donate electrons spontaneously to cupric ions, establishing that \(\mathrm{Zn} > \mathrm{Cu}\). Combining both comparative results establishes the overall activity series for electron release: \(\mathrm{Zn} > \mathrm{Cu} > \mathrm{Ag}\).

Step 5: Final Answer
Copper releases electrons to silver ions, showing that copper is oxidised to cupric ions while silver ions are reduced to silver metal, establishing the electron-releasing tendency as \(\mathrm{Cu} > \mathrm{Ag}\).

answer.text: Silver releases electrons to copper, showing that silver is oxidised while copper(II) ions are reduced, establishing that silver has a higher electron-releasing tendency than copper.
Both copper and silver metals undergo oxidation simultaneously, showing identical electron-releasing tendencies.
Copper releases electrons to silver ions, being oxidised to cupric ions while silver ions are reduced to silver metal, establishing the electron-releasing tendency as \(\mathrm{Cu} > \mathrm{Ag}\).
Copper is reduced to cuprous oxide causing the blue coloration, while silver nitrate is oxidised to nitrogen dioxide gas.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q04 - Structural oxidation states of tribromooctaoxide

questiontext.text:
The structural arrangement of tribromooctaoxide (\(\mathrm{Br}_3\mathrm{O}_8\)) is depicted below:

Based on the chemical structure shown, what are the individual oxidation states of the terminal and central bromine atoms, and what is the average oxidation state of bromine in this molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Representation of Tribromooctaoxide
The Lewis structure of \(\mathrm{Br}_3\mathrm{O}_8\) consists of a linear chain of three bromine atoms: \(\mathrm{O}_3\mathrm{Br}-\mathrm{BrO}_2-\mathrm{BrO}_3\). Each terminal bromine atom is bonded to three oxygen atoms through coordinate/double bonds and to one adjacent bromine atom via a homonuclear covalent single bond. The central bromine atom is bonded to two oxygen atoms and two neighboring bromine atoms.

Step 2: Assignment of Oxidation States by Bond Cleavage Rules
By definition of oxidation state, the shared electron pair in a covalent bond is formally assigned entirely to the more electronegative partner: 1. For each \(\mathrm{Br}=\mathrm{O}\) bond, oxygen is more electronegative than bromine; hence, each bond to oxygen contributes \(+2\) to bromine. 2. For the \(\mathrm{Br}-\mathrm{Br}\) homonuclear bonds, both atoms have identical electronegativities; hence, the electron pair is divided equally, contributing \(0\) to each bromine atom's oxidation state.

Step 3: Calculating Individual Oxidation States
- For each terminal bromine atom: each is bonded to three oxygen atoms and one bromine atom. Therefore, the oxidation state is \(3 \times (+2) + 0 = +6\).
- For the central bromine atom: it is bonded to two oxygen atoms and two bromine atoms. Therefore, the oxidation state is \(2 \times (+2) + 0 = +4\).

Step 4: Calculation of Average Oxidation State
The average oxidation number of bromine in the neutral molecule is:
\(\text{Average} = \frac{(+6) + (+4) + (+6)}{3} = +\frac{16}{3}\).
This rationalises the paradox of fractional oxidation states: electrons are never transferred in fractions; the non-integer value of \(+\frac{16}{3}\) simply represents the stoichiometric average of atoms present in two different whole-number oxidation states (\(+6\) and \(+4\)).

Step 5: Final Answer
Each terminal bromine atom is in the \(+6\) oxidation state, the central bromine atom is in the \(+4\) oxidation state, and the average oxidation state of bromine is \(+16/3\).

answer.text: Each terminal bromine atom is in the \(+4\) oxidation state, the central bromine atom is in the \(+6\) oxidation state, and the average oxidation state is \(+14/3\).
All three bromine atoms possess an identical fractional oxidation state of \(+16/3\) because the electrons are equally delocalised.
Each terminal bromine atom is in the \(+7\) oxidation state, the central bromine atom is in the \(+2\) oxidation state, and the average oxidation state is \(+16/3\).
Each terminal bromine atom is in the \(+6\) oxidation state, the central bromine atom is in the \(+4\) oxidation state, and the average oxidation state is \(+16/3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q05 - Structural analysis of sulfur in tetrathionate

questiontext.text:
The structural formula of the tetrathionate anion (\(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\)) is shown below:

Which of the following statements correctly rationalises the individual oxidation states of the sulfur atoms and accounts for the observed fractional average value of \(+2.5\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Layout of Tetrathionate
The structural formula of the tetrathionate ion \(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\) shows a linear core of four sulfur atoms: \([^{-}\mathrm{O}_3\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{S}^*-\mathrm{S}^*-\mathrm{SO}_3^-]\). The two terminal sulfur atoms are bonded to oxygen atoms, whereas the two inner sulfur atoms (\(\mathrm{S}^*\)) are bonded solely to other sulfur atoms.

Step 2: Assigning Oxidation Numbers to Terminal Sulfur Atoms
Each terminal sulfur atom forms: - Two double bonds with oxygen atoms (\(\mathrm{S}=\mathrm{O}\)), each contributing \(+2\) because oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur. - One single bond with an \(\mathrm{O}^-\) ion, contributing \(+1\). - One single bond with a neighboring sulfur atom (\(\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{S}^*\)), contributing \(0\) because there is no difference in electronegativity between two sulfur atoms. Hence, the oxidation state of each terminal sulfur atom is:
\(\text{Oxidation state} = 2(+2) + (+1) + 0 = +5\).

Step 3: Assigning Oxidation Numbers to Inner Sulfur Atoms
Each of the two inner sulfur atoms (\(\mathrm{S}^*\)) forms two single covalent bonds exclusively with adjacent sulfur atoms (\(\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{S}^*\) and \(\mathrm{S}^*-\mathrm{S}^*\)). Because no electronegativity difference exists across any of these bonds, the electron pairs are shared equally without transfer. Thus, the oxidation state of each inner sulfur atom is strictly \(0\).

Step 4: Rationalisation of Fractional Oxidation State
Calculating the net sum of oxidation states across the four sulfur atoms gives:
\(\text{Sum} = (+5) + 0 + 0 + (+5) = +10\).
The average oxidation number is:
\(\text{Average} = \frac{+10}{4} = +2.5\).
This demonstrates that electrons are not transferred in fractions; the fractional value \(+2.5\) is simply the mathematical average of two sulfur atoms in the \(+5\) oxidation state and two sulfur atoms in the \(0\) oxidation state.

Step 5: Final Answer
Each of the two terminal sulfur atoms exhibits an oxidation state of \(+5\), each of the two central sulfur atoms exhibits an oxidation state of \(0\), and the value of \(+2.5\) is their structural average.

answer.text: Each of the two terminal sulfur atoms has an oxidation state of \(+5\), each of the two central sulfur atoms has an oxidation state of \(0\), and \(+2.5\) is their structural average.
All four sulfur atoms possess an identical non-integral oxidation state of \(+2.5\) due to continuous resonance delocalisation across the sulfur chain.
Each of the two terminal sulfur atoms has an oxidation state of \(+6\), each of the two central sulfur atoms has an oxidation state of \(-1\), yielding an average of \(+2.5\).
Each of the two terminal sulfur atoms has an oxidation state of \(+4\), while each of the two central sulfur atoms has an oxidation state of \(+1\), yielding an average of \(+2.5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q06 - Role of salt bridge and ion migration in galvanic cell

questiontext.text:
The diagram below shows the operation of the Daniell cell with details of ionic movement through the salt bridge containing potassium chloride (\(\mathrm{KCl}\)):

During the spontaneous discharge of the cell, which statement correctly describes the charge carriers in the circuit and the direction of ion migration through the salt bridge to maintain electrical neutrality?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Circuit Paths in the Daniell Cell
An operating galvanic cell comprises two interconnected circuits: 1. An external metallic circuit (wire, switch, and measuring meter). 2. An internal electrolytic circuit (electrolyte solutions and the salt bridge).

Step 2: Charge Carriers in External and Internal Circuits
- In the external metallic wire, electrical current is transported exclusively by the directed flow of free electrons travelling from the zinc electrode (anode) to the copper electrode (cathode).
- In the internal solution phase, current cannot travel via free electrons; instead, electricity is carried by the physical migration of dissolved ions across the solutions and through the salt bridge.

Step 3: Charge Imbalance in Half-Cell Beakers
- At the anode, continuous oxidation (\(\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^-\)) produces positive \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions, leading to an excess accumulation of positive charge in the anode beaker.
- At the cathode, continuous reduction (\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\)) removes positive \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions from the solution, leading to an excess of unpartnered negative sulfate ions (\(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\)) in the cathode beaker.

Step 4: Direction of Ion Migration from the Salt Bridge
To maintain electrical neutrality in both compartments and allow steady current to flow: - Anions from the salt bridge (\(\mathrm{Cl}^-\)) migrate toward the anode compartment (zinc half-cell) to neutralize accumulating \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions. - Cations from the salt bridge (\(\mathrm{K}^+\)) migrate toward the cathode compartment (copper half-cell) to neutralize excess \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\) ions.

Step 5: Final Answer
Current is carried by electrons in the external circuit from zinc to copper, and by ions in the internal circuit where anions migrate toward the zinc anode compartment while cations migrate toward the copper cathode compartment.

answer.text: Current is carried by electrons through both the external wire and the salt bridge, moving continuously from copper to zinc.

Current is carried by electrons in the external circuit from zinc to copper, and by ions in the internal circuit where anions migrate toward the zinc anode compartment and cations toward the copper cathode compartment.
Current is carried by zinc ions moving through the metallic wire to the cathode, while electrons travel across the salt bridge to complete the loop.
Current is carried by electrons in the wire from copper to zinc, while chloride anions migrate exclusively to the copper cathode to maintain neutrality.
